item.title: Republicans just got a powerful new playbook for the battle for Congress. Here's what's inside
item.description: First on Fox: Advancing American Freedom unveils over 100 proposals to cut housing, energy and healthcare costs ahead of 2026 midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: With control of Congress on the line and pocketbook issues dominating the campaign trail, a prominent conservative group is unveiling a sweeping affordability agenda aimed at giving Republicans a sharper economic message ahead of the November midterm elections.

The Advancing American Freedom report, "Affordability 101," obtained first by Fox News Digital ahead of its Capitol Hill rollout Thursday, lays out more than 100 recommendations to lower the costs of housing, energy, food and healthcare by expanding supply, increasing competition and reducing government barriers.

The blueprint is a potential resource for Republican lawmakers and congressional staff while affordability emerges as one of the defining issues of the 2026 midterm elections. Founded by former Vice President Mike Pence, Advancing American Freedom argues costs can be lowered by reducing regulations, encouraging competition and boosting domestic production rather than creating new federal subsidies.

"We want free market conservative candidates to go out there and not just put on the red jersey or not just fight against the blue jersey, but to go there and give people ideas that actually work," Advancing American Freedom President Tim Chapman told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP’S AFFORDABILITY PLAN FACES CONSERVATIVE PUSHBACK AS POCKETBOOK ISSUES LOOM OVER MIDTERMS

Chapman argued the size and scope of government plays a larger role in affordability than many Americans realize.

"The size and scope of the government matters more than people understand in terms of its impact on the economy," Chapman said. "If you look at interest rates right now and how much of the skyrocketing interest rates are fueled by the debt and deficit problem, that's something we need to be concerned about as Americans."

Many of the proposals align with Trump administration priorities, including expanding domestic energy production, building more homes, reducing regulations and encouraging innovation.

But the blueprint also breaks with the administration on several issues.

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

One flashpoint is Vice President JD Vance's proposal to expand childcare subsidies by broadening eligibility under the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), potentially providing some married families with a stay-at-home parent up to about $9,000 per child annually.

"His proposal sounds great, right?" Richard Stern, vice president of the Plymouth Institute for Free Enterprise at Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. "But the truth is, in many cases, it's a $9,000 divorce bonus."

On housing, the report says government regulations add 26.4% to the cost of a new single-family home and calls for permitting, zoning and land-use reforms to lower construction costs.

"I think those memos that deal with construction regulations and land use are the core group that would help affordability the most," Stern said.

5 STATES COULD BE THE BIGGEST LOSERS IN TRUMP'S TRADE WAR WITH CANADA, EXPERT WARNS

The report also argues tariffs raise consumer prices, another point of disagreement with the administration.

"If you look at your grocery bill, how much of that is impacted by tariffs?" Chapman said. "That's driving up the price of goods and it's hurting people in their pocketbooks."

The blueprint also argues that expanding domestic energy production and easing regulations on artificial intelligence and data centers can help lower costs. Trump has championed rapid data center development despite growing concerns over electricity demand and local impacts.

"The counties that have data centers are making money off of it," Stern said. "They're actually reducing energy prices for those homes."

As candidates sharpen their economic messages ahead of November, Chapman said the report is meant to give lawmakers concrete policy proposals they can take back to voters.

"We want people to have those solutions," Chapman said. "When they go home and talk to their constituents about the future of the country, they can say, 'I actually have an idea. Here's an idea for getting interest rates down or here's an idea for more small business growth.'"

item.title: Tennis great Patrick McEnroe urges Congress to cap foreign recruits, protect American student-athletes
item.description: Patrick McEnroe told Congress that nearly 70% of Division I tennis roster spots now go to international recruits, crowding out American kids.
item.content:encoded:
Tennis legend Patrick McEnroe took his fight directly to Capitol Hill this week, urging Congress to cap international athletes on college rosters at 20%.

Speaking with OutKick following his testimony before the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, the former Davis Cup captain made his mission clear: stop taxpayer-funded universities from shutting out American kids and restore their focus on developing young domestic talent.

"Football and basketball are essentially professional now, and universities are under increasing pressure to fund them," McEnroe told OutKick. "The sports being squeezed are tennis, wrestling and swimming, the Olympic sports that don’t generate revenue."

The turning point came when McEnroe turned on the SEC Network to watch a college tennis championship and noticed that only two of the 12 players on the court were American. An ACC championship match revealed an even worse ratio, with just one American out of 12. In Division I tennis, international recruits now occupy nearly 70% of roster spots.

"This is collegiate tennis, and we’re losing a pathway of dreams and opportunities for American kids," McEnroe said. "I think of it as the rungs on a ladder. If you keep taking away the rungs, the kids will eventually give up."

At his academy in New York, McEnroe sees young American athletes grinding every weekend, only to watch collegiate opportunities evaporate as coaches favor older international recruits with professional experience.

"Many of those kids dream of playing professionally, but by 14 or 15, they realize that probably won’t happen," McEnroe explained. "What they want is the opportunity to play college tennis, and they’re starting to see that dream disappear. I don’t think that’s right."

"That’s why I say I’m not worried about the players who are going to make it," he added. "They represent roughly 1 percent of the people who play college tennis or other college sports and eventually become professionals. This is about the masses."

CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION

To fix the system, McEnroe is backing a legislative proposal introduced by Rep. Tim Walberg, R-Mich., that would cap international roster spots at 20%. McEnroe believes a firm limit is necessary to give American student-athletes a fairer opportunity.

"I don’t believe the purpose of that funding is to give every roster spot to international athletes," McEnroe emphasized. "I’m completely in favor of international athletes participating, but there needs to be a reasonable limit."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

He noted that college coaches, trapped in a 'win-now' mentality, are often forced into the recruiting arms race, even if many privately support reform.

"I don’t blame the colleges or coaches," McEnroe said. "The system needs guardrails so American kids have an opportunity to play. If the percentage is limited, everyone is on a level playing field."

"Many coaches I know won’t publicly support this because they’re afraid of losing their jobs," he added. "That’s why I’m doing it for them. I believe most coaches want a level playing field."

For McEnroe, tennis is just the tip of the iceberg in a much broader battle across college sports.

"This is a message we should send to young athletes and families in every sport, including soccer and lacrosse," McEnroe added. "In non-revenue Olympic sports, we need to restore some balance to collegiate athletics."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The disparity is especially striking when viewed through the lens of the global stage. At the 2024 Paris Olympics, 1,200 NCAA athletes competed, but only 386 were American. More than 800 international athletes trained in U.S. collegiate programs before competing against American athletes at the Olympics.

"We have the best training, coaches, facilities and competition in collegiate sports, and we provide all of that to international athletes so they can return home and compete against us in the Olympics," McEnroe argued. "I don’t think that’s what we want taxpayer money supporting."

TRUMP URGES CONGRESS TO PASS PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT BEFORE RECESS: 'WE HAVE TO GET THAT DONE'

Capping foreign spots is not an attack on international players.

It is a necessary fix to ensure American universities return to their core mission of developing home-grown talent.

"I’m an international person," McEnroe concluded. "I’ve been fortunate to travel the world through tennis and make friends everywhere. I love that part of tennis and many other sports. But that doesn’t mean international athletes should completely take over an American collegiate athletic system."

item.title: To beat China in AI, America must work with communities — not around them
item.description: The United States faces over 200 data center moratoriums, but a proposed American AI Infrastructure Compact could protect ratepayers and communities.
item.content:encoded:
To preserve America’s national security and economic competitiveness against foreign adversaries, the United States must lead the artificial intelligence (AI) era.

But, the infrastructure necessary to maintain that edge is increasingly being questioned. More than 200 communities have enacted data center moratoriums or similar restrictions, a growing number of states are imposing or considering pauses, and dozens of high-profile data center projects have slowed or stopped across the country.

Certainly, local communities have legitimate questions about this buildout. Who pays for the new electricity and infrastructure? What happens to local water supplies? How will noise, light and large industrial facilities affect nearby neighborhoods? And what will communities receive in return? Those questions deserve and must have honest answers.

DEMOCRATS CAN TAKE THE LEAD ON ONE OF THE NATION’S TOP ISSUES – DATA CENTERS

But at the same time, America must keep building its data center infrastructure. AI is the most transformative technology of the past 100 years, one that is already driving roughly a third of U.S. economic growth. What we build, or don’t build, today will help determine whether America leads the AI era or falls behind China.

We need a better way forward. An "American AI Infrastructure Compact" can protect communities while giving responsible projects a predictable path to construction. Four key protections include:

US ADVERSARY TURNS UP THE HEAT ON AMERICA’S AI LEAD WITH AN UNDERESTIMATED EDGE

ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM

Communities have every right to demand responsible development from companies making enormous investments. The goal should be to secure those protections without turning away the jobs, investment and tax revenue responsible projects can bring.

AMERICA NEEDS AI TO SURVIVE. WORKING FAMILIES ALSO NEED TO SURVIVE IT

These commitments are not merely aspirational. One central element of this compact — protecting ratepayers — is already taking shape. In March 2026, America’s largest data center developers signed the national Ratepayer Protection Pledge, committing to build, bring or buy the power their data centers need and cover the cost of the infrastructure required to deliver it. Since then, hundreds of utilities, developers and states have joined them in this pledge.

These arrangements can do more than shield existing customers from new costs. They can also spread fixed grid costs across a larger customer base and lower rates. In Indiana, a utility has proposed a rate reduction that would save the average household roughly $100 a year, citing revenue from data centers and other large customers. In Louisiana, agreements connected to Meta’s data center will return roughly $2.6 billion to customers over two decades. And NextEra Energy has proposed $2.25 billion in bill credits for customers in Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina as it prepares to meet a pipeline of more than 130 gigawatts of large-load demand, including data centers.

But a compact has two sides. These four protections above define what communities should expect from developers. When a project meets those standards, government owes something in return: a clear and predictable path to approval and construction.

TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS'

That path requires government to set the rules before an application arrives, keep the goalposts in place and approve projects that meet the standards after adequate review. That is how trust runs both ways. Communities know their protections will be enforced, and builders know that meeting the requirements allows them to move forward.

America has done this before. The interstate highway system stalled for years over disagreements about who paid for what. Progress came when the country settled on a durable cost-sharing framework that gave every party certainty. Big national ambitions require clear responsibilities and dependable rules.

That is the bargain America needs now: Communities get enforceable protections and measurable local benefits. Responsible builders get clear rules and a predictable path to construction. America gets the infrastructure it needs to lead the AI era. That is a win-win-win.

item.title: Michigan Republican lawmaker warns guaranteed income programs do not work, voices opposition to state policy
item.description: Michigan Republicans are demanding oversight of Rx Kids, a $300 million cash assistance program they say has become a guaranteed income experiment.
item.content:encoded:
Guaranteed income programs do not work and amount to mere "redistributions of wealth," according to Michigan Republican state Rep. Jay DeBoyer, who joined other Republicans in the state Legislature in criticizing the programs, which have gained prominence in recent years.

"Absolutely not. When does that stop?" Rep. DeBoyer, R-Clay Township, told Fox News Digital. "When you think about the role of government, the role of government is not to fund people's lives. The role of the government is to provide a conducive environment where you have opportunities for success."

DeBoyer, who chairs the state House Oversight Committee, is leading a contingent of Michigan House Republicans demanding rigorous inspection of Rx Kids — a taxpayer-funded initiative billed as the nation's largest prenatal and infant cash assistance program. Lawmakers are raising alarms over how hundreds of millions of public dollars are being spent.

DIRECTOR OF 'CASH GIVEAWAY' PROGRAM TAILORED TO NEW MOTHERS GRILLED ON HOW TAXPAYER FUNDING IS USED IN DEBATE

The scrutiny boiled over during a June 2 House Oversight Committee hearing, where GOP lawmakers targeted the program’s lack of spending restrictions or income limits.

Republican leaders argue the state-funded initiative has evolved into something far different than what was originally presented to the Legislature, accusing Democrats of using hundreds of millions of dollars in public funding to advance a broader guaranteed-income agenda.

Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall told Fox News Digital that lawmakers were led to believe they were funding a targeted maternal and prenatal health initiative — not what he characterized as an open-ended social experiment. Under the current design, Rx Kids provides expectant mothers with a lump-sum payment of $1,500 during pregnancy, followed by $500 per month for six or 12 months after birth, depending on the participating community, regardless of household income.

GOP lawmakers across the country have raised similar legal, budgetary, and ideological objections to guaranteed basic income (GBI) and direct cash transfer programs.

In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Harris County over its Uplift Harris direct-cash pilot, prompting the Texas Supreme Court to block the payments in 2024. Harris County later terminated Uplift Harris and a successor program in June 2025 and moved to reallocate the funds. In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed Republican-backed legislation that would have prohibited local municipalities and counties from enacting GBI initiatives. Meanwhile, Iowa Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds signed House File 2319 into law on May 1, 2024, banning local guaranteed income programs statewide.

CALIFORNIA GUARANTEED INCOME ADVOCACY GROUP RECOMMENDS PERMANENT POLICY FUNDED BY 'DEDICATED LOCAL TAXES'

The director of Michigan's Rx Kids, Dr. Mona Hanna, told Fox News Digital that the initiative is neither a traditional guaranteed income program nor a universal basic income (UBI) model, pointing to its strict focus on the critical first year of a child's life.

DeBoyer directly challenged that distinction, pointing to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) plan. The state document explicitly defines a "guaranteed income program" as a "cash payment provided on a regular basis to members of a community with no strings attached and no work requirement," citing Rx Kids as a primary example.

"The truth is this is just about redistribution of wealth," DeBoyer said. "It's a distribution tactic that I would argue is not going to help moms and babies, when that's actually what we should be trying to do."

Progressive advocates have pushed back against the Republican offensive. Adriane Brown, senior communications director for the Economic Security Project (ESP) — an advocacy group founded in 2016 to promote direct cash transfers — argued that direct assistance enjoys bipartisan support.

"Cash is widely supported across ideological lines, and there’s long been growing momentum and political appetite for guaranteed income," Brown told Fox News Digital.

"The majority of the Michigan Legislature supports this pilot," Brown added. "Republican Senator John DaMoose wrote an op-ed in the Detroit Free Press about how Rx Kids is a pro-life policy and ‘fiscally responsible,’ and the program has been expanded in both urban and rural communities throughout Michigan by both Democrat and Republican leaders."

GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE

Brown emphasized that economic pressures on young families necessitate immediate, flexible relief.

"The bottom line is, people are struggling in our economy," Brown said. "It’s more expensive than ever to have a child. In acute moments of vulnerability, people need all the support they can get. It doesn’t make sense to malign cash assistance as a partisan idea when so many communities would benefit from the stability it offers."

Meanwhile, the ESP has been pushing for guaranteed income long before affordability became a salient issue. Founded in 2016, ESP launched with more than "100 entrepreneurs, activists, researchers and philanthropists" advocating for direct cash payments.

The ESP helped create over 100 guaranteed income pilots across the U.S.

The broader campaign for direct payments includes Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, led by former Stockton, California, Mayor Michael Tubbs. Tubbs, who launched one of the nation's early municipal cash experiments, has long argued that federal tax dollars should fund income supplements to help lower-income Americans keep up with rising inflation, rent and groceries, claiming it's a viable policy to tackle affordability.

As many guaranteed income advocates would like to make the policy permanent and even push it at the federal level, only Cook County, Illinois has approved such a measure so far.

DeBoyer countered that established social safety nets already exist to support low-income families, but said those programs carry strict eligibility standards and oversight mechanisms that Rx Kids lacks.

"We have a safety net. We spend literally billions of dollars on social welfare," DeBoyer said. "The difference is, in this particular spending, there are no parameters. There is no means test. Literally a millionaire qualifies for this program. An individual who's not an American citizen qualifies for this program."

"An individual that is in this program can spend their money on anything they want to spend their money on — they can spend it on alcohol, cigarettes, fast-food or vacations. At the end of the day, we can say that this is about moms and babies, but that creates the potential for massive abuse."

item.title: Craig Carton: 'Crazy people' hate Sydney Sweeney, support Lindsay Clancy
item.description: Craig Carton divided critics into two camps, contrasting outrage over the Sydney Sweeney Novig ad with those who he says supported Lindsay Clancy.
item.content:encoded:
OutKick host Craig Carton addressed the difference between those who were fine with Sydney Sweeney showing some skin in a sports advertisement and those who supported Lindsay Clancy during her trial in the killings of her three children.

Carton, who hosts "The Craig Carton Show" on OutKick, put it bluntly when addressing the so-called Sweeney controversy over her ad for Novig.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"The world’s going crazy when it comes to the photographs of Sydney Sweeney. ‘Oh, we’re sexualizing women. It’s not right. It’s setting the women’s movement back 100 years.’ No, you’re just ugly. That’s what that is."

Female athletes and some in the media wagged their finger at Sweeney and Novig over the ad, which showed the actress nearly nude talking about all of the sports users could wager on with the company.

Carton asserted that the same ones who were upset about the Sweeney spot also thought Clancy was a "hero."

"I’m gonna separate people into two groups, OK? There’s going to be here on the left side, crazy people. We’re gonna call you ‘crazy.’ On the other side, I’m just gonna refer to you as not crazy," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Consider for a moment that the non-crazy side loves those pictures of Sydney Sweeney. The crazy side would rather support, I don’t know, Lindsay Clancy. She’s a hero to the crazy side. I saw one of those gals come out this morning legitimately refer to her as heroic. She killed her three children. She killed her own children. But for the crazies, ‘Man, she gets it. She represents us.’ For the non-crazies, she belongs in prison for the rest of her life.

"Crazy people hate Sydney Sweeney. Crazy people love Clancy. Non-crazy people love Sydney Sweeney. Non-crazy people think Clancy should be behind bars for the rest of her life."

Earlier this month, the jury in the Clancy trial was deadlocked with one juror holding out on a not guilty determination. Massachusetts Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial as the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict in the case.

Clancy had been charged with first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths of her children, each of whom had been strangled with exercise bands.

Sweeney only riled up some people with an advertisement.

item.title: San Diego bystanders chase down suspected Tesla thief after woman struck on boardwalk
item.description: Video captured on smart glasses shows bystander Alex Srour chasing down a suspect who allegedly drove a stolen Tesla through a San Diego pedestrian walkway.
item.content:encoded:
Bystanders chased down and tackled a suspected car thief after he allegedly drove a stolen Tesla through a crowded San Diego pedestrian walkway, striking a woman and leaving her with serious injuries.

Video shows Juan Antonio Gonzaba, 39, fleeing the vehicle, which police told numerous local media outlets was stolen, and sprinting through a parking lot.

Bystander Alex Srour leaped into action, chasing Gonzaba down and pushing him while he ran, resulting in Gonzaba falling to the ground.

SUSPECTED DUI DRIVER LEADS COPS ON WILD CHASE BEFORE DRAMATIC TAKEDOWN ON POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH

"I hear somebody behind me just scream like, ‘Watch out.’ And then I look and there's like a Tesla just barreling at me going like 70 miles an hour," Srour told KABC-TV.

Police charged Gonzaba with assault with a deadly weapon, hit-and-run and auto theft in connection with the incident, according to the San Diego Sheriff's Office.

JEANINE PIRRO REVEALS HOW HIGH-TECH CAR THIEVES 'REWRITE THE BRAIN’ OF VEHICLES AND SHIP THEM OVERSEAS

Srour, who recorded the incident on a pair of smart glasses he was wearing, said he was sideswiped when Gonzaba careened the Tesla down a pedestrian boardwalk.

"He hit my bike, and it like pushed me really, it like launched me off to the side," Srour told KABC, adding, "People don't expect a car to come through the boardwalk like it's just not normal."

WATCH: BYSTANDERS, POLICE LIFT VOLKSWAGEN OFF WOMAN PINNED UNDERNEATH AFTER DRAMATIC E-BIKE CRASH

Gonzaba allegedly struck a 25-year-old woman, who was transferred to the hospital with injuries that included a fractured spine, broken ribs and a cut that required 20 stitches, prosecutors told KNSD-TV.

Gonzaba is being held without bail in the San Diego Central Jail after prosecutors noted that he has an extensive criminal history, KNSD reported.

'TESLA ROAD RAGE DRIVER' SENTENCED TO SEVEN YEARS IN PRISON AFTER ATTACKING MOTHER AND DAUGHTER IN HAWAII

If convicted on all charges, Gonzaba faces up to 24 years in prison, prosecutors said Wednesday. Gonzaba pleaded not guilty to all charges during his arraignment, KNSD reported.

Fox News Digital contacted the San Diego Police Department and the San Diego District Attorney's Office for further comment.
